Lessons.Title: Thousandths on Grids and in Words
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM K5 2021 G5 U05:L02 Thousandths on Grids and in Words: name and draw decimal units to THREE decimal places on a consistent whole. The source asks pupils to shade provided numbers, interpret actual shaded publisher grids, and critique competing verbal place-value interpretations. Correct digits without the original grid cannot prove drawing competence.

Warm-up source Estimation Exploration What Part of the Square is Shaded uses an original source image with unknown precise shaded fraction in HTML; low/about-right/high estimates remain teacher reviewed. Do not invent exact original warm-up shading from a different first-party image.

Activity 1 Represent Thousandths on a Grid original source prompts: shade a.2/10=0.2, b.0.2, c.15/100=0.15 and d.0.34. Interpret four additional source diagrams a–d: only the fourth diagram's HTML alt description independently states 62 of100 hundredth cells shaded and five of ten small pieces of another hundredth cell, so that described diagram represents0.625; other source diagrams' precise shading requires original visual review. Last original student task says SHADE0.328 on the grid, then explain 3 tenths,2 hundredths,8 thousandths.

Activity 2 Say What?: student representations for source-shaded FIFTEEN HUNDREDTHS=0.15. Jada says15 hundredths (correct), Priya150 thousandths (correct), Tyler15 thousandths (INCORRECT:0.015), Diego1 tenth and5 hundredths (correct), Mai1 tenth and half a tenth (correct). Teacher reviews WHY representations of the SAME whole agree and why Tyler switches denominator.

An independently authored teacher-scored Cool-down asks pupils to shade0.437 and justify the 7 thousandths. Exact Practice family covers source-decimal choice and Jada/Priya/Tyler/Diego/Mai conceptual answer values only. Original figure interpretation and freehand source drawings remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Gated source Cool-down cannot be certified; existing other mathematically correct first-party example 0.327 is retained as optional extension.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: use a consistent whole, a hundredths grid and a further division of hundredths into tenths to read, represent and name decimal thousandths. The lesson explicitly asks learners to move among shaded areas, decimals, fractions and written place-value language.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: a source-style unit square with roughly three quarters shaded, but no grid, does not provide an exact count. Offer a too-low estimate such as one half, an about-right estimate such as three quarters, and a too-high estimate such as nine tenths, then explain why a hundredths grid would refine the estimate. These are illustrative estimates, not recovered values from the publisher image.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — partition to thousandths: draw a 10 by 10 unit grid and treat every square as one hundredth of the whole. Subdivide one hundredth into ten equal strips. Each strip is one thousandth of the same original whole. Represent 0.327 by three whole tenths, two separate hundredths, and seven thousandth-strips; compare that with 327 of 1000 equal-area parts.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — multiple names: explain 0.625 as 625 thousandths or 6 tenths, 2 hundredths, and 5 thousandths. Explain that 0.15 equals fifteen hundredths or 150 thousandths, but NOT fifteen thousandths, which is 0.015. Use a labeled accessible 10×10 grid description when an actual drawing is unavailable.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment boundary: the source requires drawings, estimation discussion, alternative representations and explanations of the unit whole. A single correct decimal may be checked automatically, but whether the student's drawing has congruent parts and correct selected area remains teacher-reviewed. No source grid image or protected response is copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Hundredth into ten thousandths
KeyConcepts.Definition: One hundredth of a common whole can be subdivided into ten equal pieces.

KeyConcepts.Title: Expanded decimal meaning
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each digit identifies how many units of one decimal place value contribute to the number.
KeyConcepts.Example: A whole is fixed when changing between decimal fractions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent denominations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Decimals can be renamed without changing value if each part is exchanged at the correct rate.
KeyConcepts.Example: Zero padding on the right does not change a decimal.

Lessons.Title: Thousandths in Expanded Form
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 Grade5 U05:L03 Thousandths in Expanded Form: connect grid-shaded original whole with each digit's decimal place-value term (tenths, hundredths, thousandths), write STANDARD and expanded decimal forms and critique a wrong claim about the zero hundredths place. A pure number answer cannot demonstrate the pupil's original shaded grid model.

Warm-up Which One Doesn't Belong source four EXPRESSIONS: 26÷100=0.26; 0.26; 26×0.001=0.026; and(2×0.1)+(6×0.01)=0.26. Numerically the 26×0.001 expression differs; students may legitimately find structural differentness in other representations, with reasoned WODB explanations reviewed by teacher.

Activity 1 Expanded Form: printed shaded source original (4×0.1)+(1×0.01)+(9×0.001) =0.419. Teacher shows original shaded drawing and asks WHY this expression matches the grid. A second source asks pupil to shade (8×0.1)+(3×0.01)+(5×0.001)=0.835, write decimal form and explain the constant whole.

Same Activity1 source Mai incorrectly says 0.105 equals (1×0.1)+(5×0.01), but her expression is 0.15. Correct expansion 0.105 is one tenth + ZERO hundredths + FIVE thousandths: (1×0.1)+(0×0.01)+(5×0.001). The zero placeholder matters; teacher reviews original pupil proof and correction.

Activity 2 Decimal Numbers in Numerous Ways: original asks to represent 477/1000=0.477; ONE HUNDRED THIRTY-SIX THOUSANDTHS=0.136; and (3×0.1)+(6×0.01)+(8×0.001)=0.368 in multiple representations. Learners can use fractions, decimals, expanded form, words and consistently divided grids; a correct format choice is only one component.

Original 2021 cool-down is teacher-gated and not asserted reproduced. Independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down uses 0.204 and requires a visual/word/expanded-form explanation. Exact selected family supports a bounded subset of numeric conversions, not grading original WODB reasoning, handwritten grid shading or Math Language Routine tasks.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: write decimals through the thousandths place in expanded form as a SUM of digit-times-place-value terms, and connect these expressions to words, standard notation and shaded unit-grid models. The source's opening Which One Doesn't Belong is open mathematical reasoning, not a uniquely keyed answer.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: contrast a number such as 0.26 with 26÷100, 26×0.001 and 2×0.1+6×0.01. Three of these represent 0.26 except 26×0.001=0.026. Explain multiple properties by which one expression might be an outlier (division, multiplication, a sum), so an apparently different-looking correct expression is not automatically wrong.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — expanded form: in an original example, a grid represents 0.835 as 8 tenths, 3 hundredths and 5 thousandths. Write 0.835=(8×0.1)+(3×0.01)+(5×0.001). Use a 1000-part area interpretation rather than relying only on decimal-place vocabulary.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — zeros preserve place: 0.105 has one tenth, zero hundredths and five thousandths. Compare the correct 0.1+0.005=0.105 with the tempting wrong 0.1+0.05=0.15. Try another independently authored 0.407=4×0.1+0×0.01+7×0.001 and compare with 0.47=0.4+0.07.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: numeric expansion can be checked exactly when given a specified standard form, but explaining Why One Doesn't Belong and showing a correctly shaded/partitioned whole requires teacher review. Source's original student diagram and gated teacher response are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Expanded decimal form
KeyConcepts.Definition: A number can be expressed as a sum of digits multiplied by their place-unit values.
KeyConcepts.Example: All three terms refer to the same unit whole.

KeyConcepts.Title: Zero in a decimal place
KeyConcepts.Definition: A zero contributes no quantity but fixes the position of the following digits.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent fractions and decimals
KeyConcepts.Definition: A thousandth-based decimal can also be written as a fraction over 1000.

Lessons.Title: Explore Place Value Relationships (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 Grade5 U05:L04 OPTIONAL Explore Place Value Relationships uses a BALANCE and physical standard weights0.1,0.01 and0.001 OUNCE to explore equivalent weights and how composing ten smaller place units creates a larger one. Third activity's nugget table switches units to GRAMS, which must be kept separate from the earlier ounce balance examples.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder Maintain Your Balance uses original photo of gold with James St John CC BY2.0 attribution, not copied without independent file/license review. Teacher asks students to notice and explain why distinct combinations of standard weights can balance same nugget mass.

Activity 1 Balance the Weight source: nugget0.2 ounce can use two0.1-ounce pieces, twenty0.01-ounce pieces, or200×0.001; multiple answers legitimate. For source0.385 ounce, minimal number of allowed0.1/0.01/0.001 pieces is3+8+5=16, maximum385 all thousandth pieces; mixed count examples are teacher-reviewed. Conversions printed:266 of0.001=0.266oz,150 of0.01=1.5oz,27 of0.1=2.7oz.

Activity 2 Weights and Place Values original: three tenths+five hundredths+eight thousandths=0.358oz; six tenths+two thousandths=0.602oz; six tenths+two hundredths=0.62oz; two hundred eighty-three thousandths=0.283oz; four hundred nine thousandths=0.409oz. The source asks digits of0.527oz, which are5 tenths,2 hundredths,7 thousandths.

Activity 3 Comparing Place Values with Weights: ten0.01-ounce pieces balance one0.1-ounce piece, and one hundred0.001-ounce pieces do too. The source GRAM nugget table says A0.6g,B0.06g,C0.006g, with ratios A/B10,A/C100,C/B1/10,C/A1/100. These relationships are based on relative unit magnitudes, not physical count of all pieces.

Numeric selected Practice includes only source exact conversions and ratios; original hands-on balance, alternative optimal weight combinations, MLR partner explanations and photograph remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down uses0.406oz.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: use a balance model to investigate equivalence of tenths, hundredths and thousandths of an ounce and explain that the SAME mass can be made from different collections of standard weights. The source is an optional exploration, not a prescription that one coin-like combination must be supplied.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: examine an original balance description: one weight of 0.01 ounce is balanced by ten separate 0.001-ounce weights. Explain why this is possible and why the number of pieces on either pan differs even though the total mass is equal. The original publisher's scale illustration and gold-nugget photograph are not reproduced.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — balance a target: assemble 0.385 ounce with denominations 0.1, 0.01, and 0.001 ounce. A place-value arrangement is three 0.1s, eight 0.01s and five 0.001s. Their combined mass is 0.385 ounce, and the arrangement uses 16 physical weights. Compare with two 0.1s, eighteen 0.01s and five 0.001s (25 weights), which balances the same mass.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — fewest and most weights: assuming an unlimited supply of only those three positive denominations and no other restrictions, 16 weights is the MINIMUM, since exchanging ten smaller pieces for one larger decreases count. Using exclusively 0.001-ounce weights gives 385 weights, the MAXIMUM because every piece must weigh at least 0.001 ounce. State the supply assumption and justify with place-value exchanges instead of just reporting the numbers.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher assessment: discussing alternate valid combinations, selecting minimal/maximal counts under declared constraints, explaining balanced masses and any physical or drawn scale representation require human review. A numeric answer is one subskill but is not an auto-pass for source exploration.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal mass with unequal piece counts
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different standard decimal-unit weights can sum to the same total mass.

KeyConcepts.Title: Place value mass sum
KeyConcepts.Definition: The count of each denomination multiplies its fractional-ounce mass.
KeyConcepts.Example: Sixteen weights in the standard denomination arrangement.

KeyConcepts.Title: Optimize number of pieces
KeyConcepts.Definition: Given only positive denominations 0.1,0.01,0.001 and unlimited supply, each ten-to-one exchange reduces count by nine.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For 0.385 oz, minimum 3+8+5=16 and maximum 385 weights.
KeyConcepts.Example: The bounds depend on the available weight sizes.

WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value model with independently checkable decimal arithmetic and an accessible description.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Prove count limits
WorkedExamples.Question: What are least and greatest numbers of weights for 0.385 oz under the three-denomination unlimited-supply rules?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value model with independently checkable decimal arithmetic and an accessible description.
Steps: To minimize pieces exchange ten smaller weights for one larger until each smaller-place count is below ten.
To maximize pieces replace all larger weights with individual 0.001 weights.
Compute both totals and check their mass.
WorkedExamples.Check: At least 385 thousandths are needed; every item has mass at least one thousandth. Exchange of larger units proves the minimum.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume equal balance requires equal numbers of weights
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Balances compare total mass, not piece count.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Sum piece count times mass for each denomination.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim a minimum or maximum without specifying supply rules
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Different available denominations or limited stocks can change extreme counts.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State that only 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 ounce weights are available in unlimited supply.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mix up 0.602 and0.62, or report ounce-mass quantities as grams in source Activities1 and2
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source explicitly distinguishes two hundredths vs two thousandths, and grams only appear in Activity3's nugget table.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Preserve decimal zeros, original ounce units and separate gram ratio comparisons with a consistent whole.

Lessons.Title: Compare Decimals
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 Grade5 Unit5 Lesson5 Compare Decimals: compare decimals to three places using equal place-value columns, and interpret what greater or smaller means in context. Farther FRISBEE means larger measured distance; faster SWIM means smaller time. The printed original values are crucial.

Warm-up original TRUE OR FALSE: 7.06=7.006 FALSE because7.060≠7.006;7.06=7.060 TRUE because zero thousandths does not change number;7.06=7.600 FALSE because tenths differ. Teacher scores student explanation of each equality and alignment.

Activity 1 Farther and Faster original: Diego throws a frisbee5.10 meters, Jada5.01 meters, so Diego wins distance. Tyler swims in35.15 seconds, Han35.30 seconds, so TYLER is faster despite his time being numerically SMALLER. Source asks the reasons, not just identity recognition.

Activity 2 Farthest Frisbee Flight: original Diego5.1m and Jada5.01m. Give TWO valid DIFFERENT distances each: Han farther than Diego, Tyler farther than Diego but less than6m, Mai shorter than Jada, Priya shorter than Jada but MORE than5m. Examples for Priya5.001m and5.009m, demonstrating the need for THOUSANDTHS between5.000 and5.010. These are independently chosen valid exemplars; source specifies INEQUALITIES, not one numeric key.

Source also asks how to reason between5.000 and5.010 and justify various answers; open intervals, decimal zeros and measurement explanations are TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Earlier mathematically valid fictional frisbee values6.207 etc are preserved only as optional practice extensions. Independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down uses original decimals not from source and teacher-reviews explanation.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: compare thousandth-place decimals using matching place-value positions, and interpret what greater or smaller means IN CONTEXT. The source distinguishes a farther frisbee throw (larger distance wins) from a faster swim (smaller recorded time wins).

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up — true or false: 7.06=7.006 is false because 7.060 has 60 thousandths but 7.006 has 6; 7.06=7.060 is true because adding a trailing zero does not change the value; 7.06=7.600 is false because the tenths digit differs. Ask learners to justify each place rather than count printed digits.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — distance versus time: an original frisbee contest records throws of 6.207,6.270 and6.199 meters. A longer distance wins, so 6.270 is best. A swimming race records 27.213,27.231 and27.208 seconds; the smaller time wins, so 27.208 is fastest. Compare aligned thousandths in each case and explain why the desired ordering reverses with the context.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — construct between numbers: choose TWO different thousandth-place decimals strictly between 5.000 and5.010, such as5.002 and5.009, then compare them. Show that a hundredth-only decimal cannot supply a value strictly between these endpoints unless finer fractional places are introduced. Several valid pairs exist.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: exact comparisons and inequality signs can be checked, but justification, benchmark use, source sport context and choosing different correct decimals are teacher-reviewed. A numeric rank alone does not certify why the result is best in its domain.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare by place value
KeyConcepts.Definition: Decimals should be compared from greatest to least place, with equivalent trailing-zero forms when useful.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three decimal digits do not always mean a larger value.

KeyConcepts.Title: Direction depends on context
KeyConcepts.Definition: Larger distances represent farther throws, but smaller times represent faster finishes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For comparable distances maximize measure; for times minimize the duration.
KeyConcepts.Example: 6.270 meters is farther than6.207, while27.208 seconds is faster than27.231.

KeyConcepts.Title: Numbers between decimals
KeyConcepts.Definition: Thousandth increments produce values strictly between consecutive hundredth values.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two or more answers may satisfy a construction task.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source decimal equalities
WorkedExamples.Question: Determine truth of 7.06=7.006,7.06=7.060,7.06=7.600.
WorkedExamples.Method: Line up ones,tenths,hundredths,thousandths, adding trailing zeros as needed.
Steps: 7.600 has six tenths; 7.060 has zero tenths, not equal.
WorkedExamples.Check: Zeros at END of fractional decimal don't change its value.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source Diego/Jada and Tyler/Han
WorkedExamples.Question: Who throws farther: Diego5.10m or Jada5.01m? Who swims faster: Tyler35.15s or Han35.30s?
WorkedExamples.Method: Larger distance but shorter elapsed time win.
Steps: Explain distinct desired ordering for distance and time.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Diego throws farther; Tyler swims faster.
WorkedExamples.Check: Physical units and direction of comparison matter.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original source open Priya interval
WorkedExamples.Question: Find TWO values more than5m but less than Jada5.01m.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the thousandths between5.000 and5.010.
Steps: Numerous valid values, requiring teacher-reviewed explanation.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Examples 5.001m and5.009m; not a unique key.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both are strictly inside required interval.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Assess decimal statements
WorkedExamples.Question: Which are true: 7.06=7.006,7.06=7.060,7.06=7.600?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value model with independently checkable decimal arithmetic and an accessible description.
Steps: Compare 7.060 with 7.006: the hundredths digits differ.
WorkedExamples.Check: Only adding a zero in the final thousandth place preserves value.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Distance and swimming rankings
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the farther throw among 6.207,6.270,6.199 meters and fastest swimmer among27.213,27.231,27.208 seconds.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value model with independently checkable decimal arithmetic and an accessible description.
Steps: For throws choose the largest decimal; 6.270>6.207>6.199.
State units and why the rankings use opposite directions.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Farther throw: 6.270 meters. Fastest swim: 27.208 seconds.
WorkedExamples.Check: The unit and the performance objective determine the comparison.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Choose two between
WorkedExamples.Question: Find two distinct decimal thousandths strictly between 5 and5.01.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value model with independently checkable decimal arithmetic and an accessible description.
Steps: Choose 5.002 and5.009, each with a thousandths digit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Compare decimals by the number of digits printed
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Trailing zeros do not change numerical value and earlier place values determine order.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Align or pad decimal places to thousandths and compare left to right.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume a larger sport measurement always wins
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Some competitions reward shorter times rather than longer distances.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify whether the context seeks a maximum length or minimum duration.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use invented6.207-meter frisbee and27.213-second swim as printed original data
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Printed source uses Diego5.10/Jada5.01m and Tyler35.15/Han35.30s and asks a thousandths interval.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore four named source measures and all open constraints; retain invented examples only as optional extensions.

SummaryPoints: Original warm-up three decimal equalities: false,true,false.
Diego5.10m > Jada5.01m, so Diego throws farther.
Tyler35.15s < Han35.30s, so Tyler swims faster.
Source Activity2 asks TWO values per 4 open relative-distance constraints, not one answer.
Priya can throw5.001m or5.009m between5m and5.01m; teacher checks source explanation.
Optional prior: Align and compare tenths, hundredths and thousandths, not numeral length.
Optional prior: A distance and a race time can require opposite ranking directions.
Optional prior: Several choices between two decimal endpoints may be valid and need a reasoned justification.

Lessons.Title: Compare Decimals on the Number Line
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: represent and compare decimals to thousandths on appropriately SCALED NUMBER LINES. The source uses nested number lines 0–1 by tenths, 0–0.1 by hundredths, and 0–0.01 by thousandths, explicitly connecting a zoomed-in segment to the next finer scale.

Warm-up — notice and wonder: read a first-party text model of three lines whose endpoints are 0–1,0–0.1,0–0.01 and whose tick intervals are 0.1,0.01 and0.001 respectively. Explain that 0.001 can be plotted exactly on the thousandths line, but requires estimation between the first two ticks on a line marked only by tenths or hundredths.

Activity 1 — interpret a zoomed interval: draw a new number line from 0.530 to0.540 with marks every 0.001. Locate 0.534 on the fourth tick after0.530 and0.537 on the seventh. Explain 0.534<0.537 and compare their difference as three thousandths. The tick scale is part of the mathematical task, not incidental decoration.

Activity 2 — compare pairs on consistent scales: compare 0.230 to0.216 by rewriting0.23=0.230 and using a 0.210–0.240 line with thousandth precision. Compare0.2 with0.02 on a 0–0.3 line with hundredth marks, noting a difference of0.18; do not reverse the coordinates of tick placements when zooming.

Assessment: teacher reviews student's selection of endpoints, tick increments and exact placements as well as explanation. An isolated greater-than symbol is not enough for the original scaled line work. Publisher's nested number-line image and gated Cool-down are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Number line scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: A marked interval represents a declared equal numerical step, and position is measured against labeled endpoints.
KeyConcepts.Rule: From0.530 to0.540 with0.001 ticks, 0.534 is four ticks after0.530.
KeyConcepts.Example: The same drawing width can represent different numerical distances at different zoom levels.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nested lines magnify place value
KeyConcepts.Definition: A smaller endpoint interval with smaller tick units makes thousandths individually visible.
KeyConcepts.Example: 0.001 is the first thousandth mark from 0 on the finest line.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare locations
KeyConcepts.Definition: A larger decimal lies farther to the right on a standard increasing number line.
KeyConcepts.Example: Choose a line capable of displaying the difference.

WorkedExamples.Title: Plot two close decimals
WorkedExamples.Question: Locate 0.534 and0.537 on a line running 0.530–0.540 in steps of0.001.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value model with independently checkable decimal arithmetic and an accessible description.
Steps: Count four equal thousandth ticks for0.534 and seven for0.537.
Explain their left-to-right order and difference.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 0.534 is left of0.537, which is larger by0.003.

WorkedExamples.Title: Choose a sufficiently fine scale
WorkedExamples.Question: Which nested line shows 0.001 exactly as a marked tick:0–1 by0.1,0–0.1 by0.01, or0–0.01 by0.001?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value model with independently checkable decimal arithmetic and an accessible description.
Steps: Observe0.001 equals one of the smallest line's intervals.
Choose the line where0.001 is exactly one step from zero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare decimals with unequal places
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare0.23 with0.216 and0.2 with0.02.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party place-value model with independently checkable decimal arithmetic and an accessible description.
Steps: State both directions with the same whole and scale.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignore the number line's tick labels when placing thousandths
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A tick may represent tenths, hundredths or thousandths according to the declared scale.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Read endpoint labels and interval increments before marking a point.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Plot a thousandth as a tenth
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The place values differ by a factor of one hundred.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use0–0.01 with one-thousandth increments when precise position is required.

SummaryPoints: Nested decimal lines change the magnitude of the displayed interval and the tick step.
Choose a scale fine enough to locate and compare thousandths.
Teacher reviews number line construction and explanation, not only numerical comparison.
